newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-ATHLETES ATTACK IAAF DECISION TO REDUCE DRUGS BAN.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-ATHLETES ATTACK IAAF DECISION TO REDUCE DRUGS BAN.

text.p: International athletics authorities came under immediate fire from their own athletes on Thursday after cutting the ban for serious drugs offences from four to two years.
On the second day of its two-day congress, the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) voted by 112 to 56 to halve their ban for performance-enhancing drugs such as anabolic steroids.

In further encouragement for athletes wishing to enhance illegally their performances and commercial potential, the congress decided to drop their three-month ban for stimulants and replace it with a "public warning" for first offenders.
The IAAF has been put in an impossible position after fighting a losing and financially disastrous war with civil courts who have ruled that four-year bans represent unacceptable restraint of trade.
"In this world it is not possible to enforce that rule," said general secretary Istvan Gyulai. "The basic rule of sport is to have equal treatment."
But former Olympic and world 100 metres champion Linford Christie said he was not convinced.
"I really don't understand," Christie said. "If we really want to eradicate drugs it should be eight years to life."
Olympic and world high hurdles champion Allen Johnson also condemned the move.
"It is not a good idea," Johnson said. "Someone could take drugs now and still get back for the Olympics. The IAAF should have zero tolerance to drugs."
Two days before the sixth world championships open here, Michael Johnson made his first public appearance for the shoe company who pay him $2,000,000 a year to promote their product.

Johnson, allowed to take part here as the defending 200 and 400 metres champion after failing to compete at the U.S. championships through injury, said he was fit and unsurprisingly defended the IAAF decision to award him a wild card.
"I think it's positive for everyone," he said.

U.S. officials said defending 100 metres champion Gwen Torrence had withdrawn from the championships without givng a reason and confirmed Gail Devers would anchor the 4x100 metres relay team with American champion Marion Jones running the second leg.
Torrence and Devers, the 1993 and 1995 world high hurdles gold medallist and current Olympic 100 champion, were both awarded wild cards.
